title: gp2Scale: A Class of Compactly Supported Non-Stationary Kernels and Distributed Computing for Exact Gaussian Processes on 10 Million Data Points
claim: Approximate scalable methods oversmooth local structure and misstate uncertainty, while ours matches the exact full model.
layout: 6 panels in 2x3 grid, shared legend on top, same axes
description: A 2x3 grid of line plots, with one shared legend above. The legend lists red training points, a black predicted mean, a gray 3-sigma confidence band and a blue true function. Each panel fits the same oscillating 1-D function. Its amplitude and frequency grow toward the right. Panel titles are SVGP, VNNGP, SKI, Vecchia, gp2Scale and BaseGP. In the top row and the Vecchia panel, the black mean follows the slow trend but smooths out the fast wiggles on the right. Gray bands are wide and irregular. VNNGP's band fills almost the whole panel. In the gp2Scale and BaseGP panels, the black mean tracks the rapid oscillations closely. Their bands are almost invisible. The eye goes first to the wide gray bands, then to the two bottom-right panels that match each other.
caption: Approximation performance of VNNGP, SVGP, SKI, Vecchia, gp2Scale, and a base regular GP for comparison, which is, in most examples we consider, computationally prohibitive. The ground truth is depicted in blue; red dots represent the training data, and the posterior mean is shown in black. VNNGP, SVGP, and SKI oversmooth and cannot adequately recover local oscillations. The Vecchia approximation shows some local oscillation, although degraded. gp2Scale best preserves local variations and sharp transitions, and offers reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) very similar to the base regular GP. Note that for all figures the posterior standard deviation of $p(f)$ is displayed, not of $p(y)$, leading to correct, vanishingly small uncertainties for the regular GP and gp2Scale, which is expected given the dense data distribution. The competing methods are clearly overestimating the uncertainty. The noise, in this example, is homoscedastic and constant across the tested methodologies.
abstract: Despite a large corpus of recent work on scaling up Gaussian processes, a stubborn trade-off between computational speed, prediction and uncertainty quantification accuracy, and customizability persists. This is because the vast majority of existing methodologies exploit various levels of approximations that lower accuracy and limit the flexibility of kernel and noise-model designs -- an unacceptable drawback at a time when expressive non-stationary kernels are on the rise in many fields. Here, we propose a methodology we term \emph{gp2Scale} that scales exact Gaussian processes to more than 10 million data points without relying on inducing points, kernel interpolation, or neighborhood-based approximations, and instead leveraging the existing capabilities of a GP: its kernel design. Highly flexible, compactly supported, and non-stationary kernels lead to the identification of naturally occurring sparse structure in the covariance matrix, which is then exploited for the calculations of the linear system solution and the log-determinant for training. We demonstrate our method's functionality on several real-world datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art approximation algorithms. Although we show superior approximation performance in many cases, the method's real power lies in its agnosticism toward arbitrary GP customizations -- core kernel design, noise, and mean functions -- and the type of input space, making it optimally suited for modern Gaussian process applications.
